title: The Fewest Colours for a Map

concept.title: Try 1, 2, 3 ... colours; never open a new colour before the previous ones are used
body: The *chromatic number* of a graph is the smallest number of colours that can colour all vertices so that **two vertices joined by an edge always get different colours**. To find it, ask "can it be done with `k` colours?" for `k = 1, 2, 3, ...` and stop at the first yes. Each question is a backtracking colouring search.

Two ideas keep the search small. First, **symmetry**: the colours have no meaning, so naming the first vertex colour 0 and the next new colour 1, and so on, loses nothing. A vertex may use the colours already in use, or **only the next unused colour**, never a colour with a larger number. Second, **order**: colour the vertices with many neighbours first, because they have the fewest choices and conflicts appear early.

body.code:
def colourable(i, k, used):                  # used: number of colours opened so far
    if i == n:
        return True
    v = order[i]
    for c in range(min(used + 1, k)):        # old colours, or the next new one
        if all(colour[u] != c for u in adj[v]):
            colour[v] = c
            if colourable(i + 1, k, max(used, c + 1)):
                return True
            colour[v] = -1
    return False

body: Without the symmetry rule the search would try every one of the `k!` renamings of each colouring. With it, each partition of the vertices into colour classes is visited once. Neighbours that are not yet coloured have colour `-1`, which never equals a real colour.

statement: A graph has `n` vertices and `m` edges. Colour the vertices so that the two ends of every edge have different colours, using as few colours as possible. Print the smallest number of colours.
inputFormat: Each of the next `m` lines has two vertices joined by an edge.
outputFormat: Print the smallest number of colours.
constraints: 0 <= m <= n * (n - 1) / 2, no repeated edges and no loops

examples.note: An odd cycle needs 3 colours; 2 are not enough.

hints: Test k = 1, 2, 3, ... and stop at the first k for which a colouring exists.
A vertex may only use a colour that is already in use, or the next new one.
Colour the vertices of large degree first.

starter.python:
n, m = map(int, input().split())
edges = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(m)]

explanation: For k = 1, 2, ... the search colours the vertices in order of decreasing degree; each vertex takes an old colour or the next new one if no neighbour has it. The first k that works is the chromatic number.
solution.complexity: Time exponential in the worst case, small for 14 vertices thanks to the symmetry rule; space O(n).
